o: Per employee we need (a) the maximum number of simultaneously active shifts and (b) the total pairwise overlap duration in minutes. Employee 1's three shifts peak at 3 concurrent (16:00–17:00) and overlap pairwise for 120+60+420 = 600 minutes. Sweep-line over start/end events gives max concurrency; pairwise interval intersection (O(m²) per employee, fine for typical data) gives total overlap. Shifts are assumed pre-converted to minute timestamps; the 'same date' clause reduces to ordinary interval overlap on the sample data.
k: Max concurrency: sweep +1 at starts, −1 at ends, track the running peak.
Total overlap duration = Σ over pairs of positive intersection length.
Sorting each employee's intervals enables both computations.

a.i: Group shifts by employee. For max concurrency, sort events (starts before ends at equal time) and track the running count. For total overlap, compare every pair of intervals and add max(0, min(ends) − max(starts)). Return results ordered by employee id.
s: Sweep events to compute the peak concurrent count.
Double loop over pairs adding positive overlaps in minutes.
Emit [employee_id, maxOverlap, totalMinutes] sorted by id.
a.t: O(E log E + Σ m_e²) — event sort dominates; pairwise overlap is quadratic per employee
a.sp: O(E) for grouped data and events

w: In real SQL you'd unpivot starts/ends into events and use a windowed running sum for max concurrency, and a self-join for pairwise durations. Pitfalls: sorting end events before start events at identical timestamps (would undercount peaks), zero-length overlaps (exclude), and shifts crossing midnight (the pairwise formula handles them naturally once times are absolute). Follow-up: compute total overlapped time per employee rather than per pair, or stream shifts online.
